curriculum.subject: Mathematics
curriculum.title: Class 6 Mathematics — Fractions
curriculum.sourceReference: Topic scope aligned to the Class 6 Mathematics fractions syllabus; all content original.

provenance.note: Authored by the Adhyaapak team. Recommend review by a subject teacher before classroom use.

concepts.title: Tenths and hundredths as fractions
concepts.description: A whole can be cut into 10 or 100 equal parts. One part is a tenth or a hundredth.
concepts.learningObjective: Write tenths and hundredths as fractions and say how many parts the whole is cut into.
concepts.teacherNote: Decimals are fractions with denominator 10, 100, 1000. If students hesitate here, return to the fraction bar before introducing the decimal point.

content.summary: Cut a bar into 10 equal parts. Each part is one tenth, written 1/10. Three parts are 3/10.
Cut each tenth into 10 smaller equal parts and the whole has 100 parts. One part is 1/100.

workedExample.problem: How many hundredths are in 2 tenths?

content.summary: Tenths and hundredths name the same amounts in different ways.
content.prompt: Write 6/10 and 60/100 on a number line from 0 to 1. What do you notice? Find another pair like this.

concepts.title: Place value in decimals
concepts.description: The digits after the decimal point are tenths, hundredths and so on. Each place is ten times smaller than the one to its left.
concepts.learningObjective: Name the place of each digit in a decimal and give its value.
concepts.teacherNote: Read decimals as place values (three point four seven), not as "three point forty-seven". The reading carries the meaning.

resources.title: The decimal point separates wholes from parts

content.summary: In 3.47 the 3 is three wholes. After the point, the 4 is four tenths and the 7 is seven hundredths.
steps: Write 3.47 in a table with columns ones, tenths, hundredths.
Put 3 under ones, 4 under tenths, 7 under hundredths.
Say it: three and four tenths and seven hundredths.

content.summary: Break a decimal into the value of each digit.
content.commonError: Treating every digit after the point as ones, so 4 in 3.47 is read as 4.

content.summary: Use place value to build and take apart decimals.
content.prompt: Use the digits 2, 5 and 9 once each to make the decimal closest to 5. Explain how place value helped you.

concepts.title: Comparing decimals
concepts.description: To compare decimals, compare the whole parts first, then tenths, then hundredths.
concepts.learningObjective: Compare and order decimals up to hundredths.
concepts.teacherNote: The trap is thinking a longer decimal is bigger (0.25 > 0.3 because 25 > 3). Write both with the same number of places: 0.25 and 0.30.

content.summary: Write both decimals with the same number of places. Then compare like whole numbers: 0.30 and 0.25.
steps: 30 is more than 25, so 0.3 is bigger than 0.25.

content.summary: Look at the tenths first. If they match, look at the hundredths.

steps: Check: 0.5 = 0.50 and 50 hundredths is more than 45 hundredths.

content.commonError: Choosing the decimal with more digits, such as 0.45 over 0.5.

content.prompt: Order 0.6, 0.06, 0.66 and 0.606 from smallest to largest. Show the method you used and check on a number line.

concepts.title: Adding decimals
concepts.description: Line up the decimal points so that tenths add to tenths and hundredths to hundredths.
concepts.learningObjective: Add decimals up to hundredths, carrying where needed.
concepts.teacherNote: Insist on lining up the decimal points. Adding 0.5 and 0.25 as 5 + 25 is the common slip.

content.summary: Tenths add to tenths, hundredths to hundredths. 0.5 + 0.25: write 0.5 as 0.50.
steps: Write 0.50 and 0.25 under each other, points lined up.

content.summary: When a place adds to 10 or more, carry to the next place on the left.
content.commonError: Adding the digits as whole numbers and writing 0.13.

content.summary: Use adding to find what is missing.
content.prompt: Find two decimals with one decimal place each that add to exactly 2.1 and where one of them is more than 1. Explain how you know.

concepts.title: Decimals and fractions
concepts.description: A decimal and a fraction can name the same amount. 0.5 is the same as 5/10 and 1/2.
concepts.learningObjective: Convert between simple decimals and fractions.
concepts.teacherNote: Watch for 0.5 read as 1/5: the digit after the point is the NUMERATOR over 10, not the denominator.

content.summary: 0.5 means 5 tenths, which is 5/10. Cut 5/10 into simplest form and you get 1/2.
Write the decimal as a fraction over 10 or 100, then simplify.
content.commonError: Reading 0.25 as 1/25, using the last digit as the denominator.

content.summary: Turn a fraction into a decimal by making the denominator 10 or 100.
content.prompt: Write 7/20 as a decimal. Then find two other fractions whose decimals are easy to find this way, and explain why.

concepts.title: Decimals in money and measures
concepts.description: Money and lengths use decimals every day: ₹3.50 is 3 rupees and 50 paise, 2.5 m is two and a half metres.
concepts.learningObjective: Solve one- and two-step problems with decimals in money and measures.
concepts.teacherNote: Let students say the problem in words first. Many errors here are about what to do, not about the decimal arithmetic.

content.summary: ₹3.50 is 3 rupees and 50 paise. Line up the points when you add money.
To find what is left, subtract the amount taken from the starting amount, lining up the points.

workedExample.problem: A rope is 3.5 m long. 1.25 m is cut off. How much is left?

content.commonError: Subtracting the smaller digit from the larger in each place, whichever is on top.

content.prompt: You have ₹20. Choose three items from a list of prices with paise so that you spend as close to ₹20 as possible without going over. Show your adding.

misconceptions.name: Reads digits after the point as ones
misconceptions.description: The student gives each digit after the decimal point its face value, as if it were a whole number.
misconceptions.recommendedExplanation: Use a place-value table with the point drawn as a bar. Each place to the right is ten times smaller. Ask: how many of these make one whole?

misconceptions.name: Thinks a longer decimal is bigger
misconceptions.description: The student compares the digits after the point as whole numbers, so 0.25 looks bigger than 0.3 because 25 is more than 3.
misconceptions.recommendedExplanation: Write both with the same number of places (0.25 and 0.30), then compare hundredths. Show them on a number line.

misconceptions.name: Adds decimal digits as whole numbers
misconceptions.description: The student adds the digits after the point as if they were whole numbers and ignores place value.
misconceptions.recommendedExplanation: Write both numbers with the decimal points lined up and the same number of places. Add tenths to tenths and hundredths to hundredths, carrying where needed.

misconceptions.name: Reads the digit as the denominator
misconceptions.description: The student turns the digit after the point into the denominator, writing 0.5 as 1/5 or 0.25 as 1/25.
misconceptions.recommendedExplanation: Read the decimal aloud as a fraction: five tenths is 5/10. The place names the denominator; the digits are the numerator.

questions.stem: Which fraction is the same as 3 tenths?
questions.explanation: Tenths means the whole is cut into 10 equal parts, so 3 tenths is 3/10.

questions.stem: 7/100 means 7 out of how many equal parts?
questions.explanation: The bottom number says how many equal parts the whole is cut into: 100.

questions.stem: In 3.47, what is the value of the digit 4?
questions.explanation: The 4 is in the first place after the point, the tenths place, so it is worth 4 tenths.

questions.stem: In 5.08, which digit is in the hundredths place?
questions.explanation: After the point come tenths (0) and then hundredths (8).
0.7 = 0.70, which is 70 hundredths. That is more than 25 hundredths.
0.5 = 0.50 = 50 hundredths, which is more than 45 hundredths. So 0.45 is smaller.

questions.stem: Which list is in order from smallest to largest?
questions.explanation: As hundredths: 25, 30, 40. So the order is 0.25, 0.3, 0.4.
0.7 is 7 tenths. 0.07 is only 7 hundredths, ten times smaller.
0.50 + 0.25: 50 hundredths and 25 hundredths make 75 hundredths, which is 0.75.
2.75 + 1.50: 75 + 50 = 125 hundredths, which is 1 whole and 25 hundredths. Ones: 2 + 1 + 1 = 4. So 4.25.
6 tenths + 7 tenths = 13 tenths = 1 whole and 3 tenths = 1.3.
0.25 = 25/100, and dividing top and bottom by 25 gives 1/4.

questions.stem: A pencil costs ₹3.50 and an eraser costs ₹2.25. What is the total cost?
A ribbon is 2.5 m long. 0.75 m is cut off. How much ribbon is left?
Meena has ₹10. She buys items costing ₹4.75 and ₹3.50. How much money is left?
